title: Practices to Decrease Parachute Science in Remote Sensing: A Case Study from South Africa
LAI Estimation using Simulated Full-Waveform Lidar Data in a Complex Forest Scene
abstract: Leaf Area Index (LAI) is a vital parameter for understanding vegetation structure , canopy complexity, and ecosystem productivity. Full-waveform LiDAR system allows the collection of continuous backscattered energy profiles that enables a more detailed characterization of canopy structure and related variations compared to traditional discrete-return LiDAR systems. By utilizing waveform-derived metrics, LAI can be estimated with improved accuracy, specially in a dense or complex vegetation. This study presents a novel approach to LAI estimation by combining multiple full-waveform-derived metrics derived from simulated NASA's Land, Vegetation, and Ice Sensor (LVIS) footprints over the Harvard Forest scene. The truth data for modeling LAI is derived through voxelization of the forest scene, leveraging the known geometry of leaves (where individual leaves are modeled as smaller facets of known dimensions) and their arrangements within the tree to determine column-based projected leaf area onto the ground, which, by definition, represents LAI. Out of 30 candidate met-rics, the optimal combination-includes (1) Gini Coefficient (GC), (2) Centroid (intensity-weighted mean), and (3) Total Return Energy (RWE). Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression using these metrics on raw waveform data produced an Adjusted R 2 of 69.4%, indicating a strong predictive relationship. Among the selected predictors, RWE (β = 2.0976, p < 0.001) had the highest positive contribution to LAI estimation, followed by Centroid (β = −2.9073, p < 0.001), while GC (β = −4.8867, p < 0.001) also showed a significant negative effect. Moreover, we investigated the impact of removing the system contribution effect using a deconvolution-based approach. This preprocessing step improved model performance, increasing the Adjusted R 2 to 72.3%, suggesting that deconvo-lution improves the predictive power of waveform-derived metrics. Noticeably, after deconvolution, GC (β = −0.3026, p = 0.743) became statistically insignificant , while RWE (β = 1.5856, p < 0.001) and Centroid (β = −2.2318, p < 0.001) remained strong predictors. Overall, this study corroborates the ability of full-waveform LiDAR combined with signal processing techniques for accurate and robust LAI estimation in complex forest environments and suggest its broader applicability for ecosystem function analysis.

title: Atmospheric correction across environmental transitions
abstract: Atmospheric correction for global-scale imaging spectroscopy must accurately characterize environmental interfaces such as coastlines, snow lines, and wildfire fronts. However, atmosphere and surface retrievals are challenging across environmental boundaries when modeling assumptions change across surface types. This poses a challenge for the next generation of wide-swath imaging spectrometers, which can limit retrieval constraints where the assumptions for the retrieval method must be generic enough for all imaged land covers. We demonstrate multi-state atmospheric correction that allows multiple surface models within the same scene, enabling optimal estimation of surface reflectance and atmospheric conditions. We leverage recent advances in forward modeling for surface reflectance retrieval and a classification from radiance to provide consistent retrievals across environmental boundaries. We focus specifically on the land-water interface by incorporating a glint model in the atmospheric correction of water pixels and a topographic model in the correction over land. We show that our multi-state atmospheric retrieval, in conjunction with these nuanced surface modeling approaches for land and water, improves consistency in surface reflectance estimates across different observation geometries while ensuring a consistent atmospheric retrieval across the land-water transition. Critically, multi-state atmospheric retrieval can be extended to include any surface-specific forward model construction, for example by including black-body temperature over fires, or using custom surface property models over snow and ice. This work will help improve the accuracy of surface reflectance retrievals and continuity of atmospheric state retrievals for high-spatial resolution airborne and space-borne imaging spectrometers operating across diverse and mixed environments.

title: BioSCape: PRISM L2A Orthocorrected Surface Reflectance
abstract:
This dataset holds Level 2A (L2A) orthocorrected, scaled surface reflectance data collected by the Portable Remote Imaging SpectroMeter (PRISM) instrument. The data were acquired in October-November 2023 for the Biodiversity Survey of the Cape (BioSCape), an international collaboration between National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) and the South African National Space Agency (SANSA) to study biodiversity in South Africa's Greater Cape Floristic Region (GCFR). PRISM is a compact image spectrometer that acquires data in the near ultraviolet (UV) to near infrared (IR) spectral bands between 350 and 1050 nanometers with 3.5-nm spectral resolution. PRISM also has a two-channel spot radiometer at short-wave infrared (SWIR) band (1240 nm and 1640 nm) in order to provide accurate atmospheric correction of the ocean color measurements. PRISM's capabilities make it well suited for studies of aquatic and coastal ecosystems. It was deployed on a NASA Gulfstream III aircraft.
This dataset holds orthocorrected surface reflectance and uncertainty in NetCDF format, quicklook images as TIFF images, and processing information in text-based YAML format.

title: BioSCape: AVIRIS-NG L3 Resampled Reflectance Mosaics, V2
abstract: This dataset holds mosaics of resampled surface reflectance from the Airborne Visible / Infrared Imaging Spectrometer-Next Generation (AVIRIS-NG) instrument for Biodiversity Survey of the Cape (BioSCape) project. AVIRIS-NG imagery was acquired in October - November 2023 over the Greater Cape Floristic Region (GCFR), South Africa. L2B surface reflectance data from these AVIRIS-NG collections were resampled to 5-m spatial resolution and mosaiced into a regular tile system of 807 tiles. A given tile includes multiple AVIRIS-NG scenes from multiple flight lines spanning multiple days. BioSCape is a multi-agency, NASA-led research project that integrates airborne imaging spectroscopy and lidar with a suite of measurements of biodiversity. The dataset includes surface reflectance with uncertainty for each tile in netCDF format along with an RGB quicklook image in TIFF format. A spatial index of mosaic grid tiles is included in GeoJSON format.

title: Monitoring Dimensions of Biodiversity in a Mega-Diverse Region of Southern Africa: from Traits to Communities to Ecosystems
abstract: The Greater Cape Floristic Region (GCFR) of South Africa includes marine and terrestrial biomes with species diversity rivaling mega-diverse tropical rainforests in a compact area (300x700km). Extinction risk studies suggest that GCFR species are among the most vulnerable to climate change over the next 50 years. I present a scoping proposal commissioned by NASA to develop a field campaign to measure and monitor the distribution and abundance of biodiversity with new remotely-sensed data and the rich historical data in this region. I will summarize the central questions to be addressed by this field campaign and lay out the proposed study design to integrate satellite, airborne, and in situ data collection. Our plan centers around the collection of new hyperspectral imagery from AVIRIS-NG, PRISM, and HyTES spectrometers combined with the LVIS laser altimeter. These data will be collected at approximately 20 m spatial resolution across much of the GCFR and nearby aquatic and marine ecosystems. These data will then be combined with existing and new observations of the spatial distribution of community composition and functional traits to enable high resolution mapping and modeling of several essential biodiversity variables (EBVs) including species distributions, functional traits (including leaf properties), and three-dimensional canopy structure. Given the wealth of available independent in situ data available that can be brought to bear, the GCFR is an ideal system to fully evaluate the capabilities of remote-sensing technology to characterize biodiversity patterns across diverse landscapes in a relatively compact geographic area. In combination with the rich historical data and well-developed ecological understanding in this region, these new observations will enable detailed exploration into the drivers and mechanisms of change including the feedbacks from changing biodiversity to regional climate, disturbance, post-fire recovery, freshwater provisioning, and other ecosystem services.

title: Monitoring Leucadendron argenteum populations: exploring opportunities offered by emerging technologies
abstract: The Cape Floristic Region hosts a range of endemic species, one of them being Leucadendron argenteum. Leucadendron argenteum is a rare, silvery leafed endemic to the Cape Peninsula. This study evaluated whether airborne hyperspectral imaging and LiDAR can reliably distinguish L. argenteum from other vegetation species in the region using NASA’s BioSCape campaign, which provided AVIRIS-NG hyperspectral imaging and LVIS LiDAR data. Seven 10 m x 10 m field plots were surveyed in validating LiDAR’s field height measurements. LiDAR waveforms were filtered, corrected for ground elevations, and used to calculate relative height metrics. LiDAR showed a positive correlation with field-measured heights. A spectral library of 26 species and 1,229 samples was vector-normalized and reduced through PCA, then passed on to XGBoost, Random Forest, Support Vector Machines (Linear and Radial Basis Function kernels), k-nearest neighbours, and logistic regression classification algorithms. As a result, L. argenteum produced a distinctive spectral signature from other sampled vegetation. XGBoost achieved the highest L. argenteum F1-score (0.631; 95 % CI: 0.519–0.733) and Random Forest the highest overall accuracy (30.7 %). A LiDAR canopy height mask (< 1 m) removed 29.6% of likely false positives. Probability mapping predicted L. argenteum occurrences across the peninsula and highlighted known populations. These results show that the integration of hyperspectral imaging and LiDAR can help monitor populations of L. argenteum across their natural range within Cape Floristic region. New technologies and instrumentation are set to facilitate long-term monitoring and management of this threatened species.

title: The Spectrum of Life
abstract: BioSCape, NASA’s first biodiversity campaign, took place in South Africa’s Greater Cape Floristic Region, a global biodiversity hotspot on land and sea. Using airborne imaging spectroscopy, lidar, and extensive field measurements, the project explored the region’s rich biodiversity, providing insights that will help us measure and monitor ecosystems from space. The Spectrum of Life is a documentary film about this groundbreaking mission, produced by Fishwater Films, a pair of ecologist/storytellers based locally in Cape Town. The film features insights from local and international researchers collaborating to push the boundaries of global biodiversity science - all weaved together with an audiovisual celebration of the region’s exceptional diversity. Check bioscape.io/film for more information.

Retrieval of Secondary Metabolites in the Erectophile-dominant Fynbos Biome from Hyperspectral Data using the PROSPECT-D Radiative Transfer Model Coupled with Machine and Active Learning Strategies
abstract: PROSPECT radiative transfer models (RTMs) have been developed to simulate leaf optical properties, with early versions such as PROSPECT-4 being widely used. However, in environments that are rich in secondary metabolites, the capabilities of these initial models may be limited due to their inability to explicitly account for the influence of such compounds. To address these limitations, PROSPECT-D was introduced, incorporating secondary metabolites like carotenoids and anthocyanins to improve modelling accuracy. Therefore, this study assessed the capability of the PROSPECT-D RTM in the Greater Cape Floristic Region (GCFR), which is very rich in secondary metabolites, to estimate carotenoids and anthocyanins. Nevertheless, RTMs often encounter challenges when confronted with datasets containing redundant or non-diverse samples, which can adversely affect model performance and prediction reliability. To address this, the machine learning regression algorithm (MLRA) Partial Least Squares Regression (PLSR) integrated with active learning (AL) techniques, namely, Pool-Based Active Learning (PAL), Cluster-Based Diversity Active Learning (CBD) and Residual Active Learning (RSAL) were utilized in this study. Without the use of active learning, PROSPECT-D inverted with PLSR yielded poor retrieval accuracies for carotenoids (R2 = 0.03; RMSE = 2253.50 µg/cm²) and anthocyanins (R2 = 0.042; RMSE = 897.76 µg/cm²). In contrast, inversions which incorporated PLSR integrated with active learning significantly improved retrievals with PAL and RSAL achieving the highest accuracies for carotenoids (R2 = 0.89; RMSE = 1.31 µg/cm²) and anthocyanins (R2 = 0.86; RMSE = 0.32 µg/cm²) respectively. These findings demonstrate that integrating RTMs with MLRA and AL techniques provide a robust framework for monitoring vegetation biochemical traits in metabolite-rich ecosystems, with implications for biodiversity conservation and ecosystem management.

title: Estimating flavonoids using radiative transfer model inversion on imaging spectroscopy data
abstract: Assessing flavonoid content is crucial for understanding plant responses to biotic and abiotic stresses. However, pigments such as chlorophylls, carotenoids, and anthocyanins, absorb light between 410 and 430 nm, thus makes it difficult to quantify flavonoid content in this region. To improve the sensitivity of flavonoids have been developed, but they are largely empirical and lack transferability across environments. Therefore, this study compares the effectiveness of the PROSAIL-D radiative transfer model (RTM) and an empirical approach in mapping flavonoids using AVIRIS data in the Fynbos biome through indices. Results show that PROSAIL-D consistently outperformed the empirical method, with the spectral index FI417,693 achieving an R2 of 0.63 and RMSE of 0.24 (mg catechin (CAE)/g). The empirical approach with the same index yielded an R2 of 0.46 and RMSE of 5.11 mg CAE/g. Overall, the RTM model demonstrated superior accuracy, with RMSE values ranging from 0.24 to 1.70, compared to 5.11 to 6.28 for empirical methods. These findings highlight the potential of integrating AVIRIS data with PROSAIL for non-destructive, remote sensing-based assessment of flavonoids, offering a scalable approach for monitoring plant health and stress responses at the canopy level.

title: BioSCape Biodiversity Across Scales [FULL DATASET]
abstract:
This project aims to observe phylogenetic, taxonomic, and functional biodiversity across ecoregions connected along the Berg and Eerste Rivers, freshwater to marine watersheds in South Africa’s Greater Cape Floristic Region. Their goal is to improve mapping of biodiversity by improving understanding of how functional diversity relates to phylogenetic and taxonomic diversity. Specifically, this project will leverage lessons learned about the spatiotemporal signal in eDNA in Californian Mediterranean-climate watersheds to address the question: how do eDNA, traditional field, and remote sensing observations of biodiversity relate across space and time? They will investigate the relationships of phylogenetic, taxonomic, and functional diversity along the Berg and Eerste Rivers, two naturally (fire and drought) and anthropogenically (dams and development) disturbed watersheds in the GCFR, a biodiversity hotspot susceptible to environmental change (climate, urbanization, etc.).

Key Project Questions
Hypothesis 1) Phylogenetic, taxonomic, and functional diversity are directly related to each other along the Berg and Eerste River systems. Hypothesis 2) Due to the hydrologic structure of watersheds, phylogenetic, taxonomic, and functional diversity self-organize spatially and are scale dependent.

title: Localized Brightness–Shape–Moisture Soil Parameterization for Improved PROSAIL-5 Canopy Simulation
abstract: The mapping and modeling of canopies is important for the understanding, monitoring, and management of vegetation systems. To effectively model or simulate canopy spectra at the hyperspectral level, background soil spectra must first be simulated accurately. Spectrometer data simulation such as this will become increasingly relevant as newer imaging spectroscopy missions such as PRISMA and AVIRIS-NG start to produce more data sets. In this study, the brightness–shape–moisture (BSM) radiative transfer model (RTM) with localized parameter distributions was used in conjunction with the PROSAIL-5 RTM to simulate canopy spectra for different biomes in the semiarid regions of Southern Africa as captured with PRISMA or AVIRIS-NG sensors. It is hypothesized that a PROSAIL-5 RTM with biome-specific BSM parameters can more accurately simulate PRISMA and AVIRIS-NG spectra than a PROSAIL-5 model simulated with the default soil spectrum, as represented by lower relative root mean square error (RRMSE) values against actual spectra. It is demonstrated that the PRISMA and AVIRIS-NG canopy spectra are more effectively simulated using their respective biome-specific BSM parameter regimes, with RRMSE improvements from 14.56% to 13.91% and from 13.64% to 10.71% for two tested images captured with these sensors.

title: Scale dependence in remotely sensed biodiversity: Leveraging continental‐scale imaging spectroscopy from the National Ecological Observatory Network
abstract: Biodiversity is under threat globally, with signiﬁcant implications for the ecosystem processes that underpin human well-being. Effective conservation efforts require scalable, replicable metrics to detect and monitor changes in biodiversity. However, a persistent challenge is deciding on the spatial scale over which to quantify biodiversity—including when using metrics derived from remote sensing—which is inherently scale-dependent. Understanding the scaling properties of remote sensing metrics is thus important for biodiversity change detection and assessment. We address this challenge by investigating the scale dependence of two remotely sensed vegetation diversity metrics, spectral richness and divergence, across 15 diverse ecosystems that are part of the United States National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON). Our continental-scale analysis builds on the success of similar studies that have shown scale dependence of spectral richness in select forest ecosystems. Our results corroborate prior ﬁndings that show that spectral richness follows well-established ecological scaling laws by adhering to the sub-linear scaling expected for species–area and functional diversity area relationships. We compare these scaling relationships to the null expectation of randomly distributed pixel values, demonstrating that empirical scaling relationships are non-random. Comparing diverse ecosystems using the same data and methods, we show how scaling parameters encode important information on the relative roles of climate, geomorphology, and ecosystem structure on vegetation-based biodiversity metrics. By advancing our understanding of the scale dependence of remotely sensed biodiversity metrics, this study lays a foundation for leveraging remote sensing data in global biodiversity monitoring and conservation.

title: A fully satellite-driven workflow for hydrodynamic modeling in data-scarce coastal systems: integrating ICESat-2, Sentinel-2, SWOT and reanalysis models
abstract: Hydrodynamic models in coastal and estuarine systems are typically constrained by sparse bathymetry, boundary, and validation data, especially in regions where field campaigns are costly or impractical. Here we develop and test a fully satellite-driven framework for hydrodynamic modeling in South Africa’s Langebaan Lagoon without using any local in situ measurements. Bathymetry is derived by training multispectral Sentinel-2 reflectance against ICESat-2 ATL24 photon-derived depths using an XGBoost model optimized with Bayesian search. The final satellite derived bathymetry reproduces independent ATL24 points with RMSE = 0.45 m and R2 = 0.97. This bathymetry was used in a depth-averaged Delft3D Flexible Mesh model driven at the open boundary by TPXO tidal harmonics and by ERA5 winds. We validate modeled water surface elevation against 16 SWOT low-rate (250 m, unsmoothed) passes in 2023. SWOT–model comparisons yield an overall RMSE of 0.11 m and R2 = 0.61, with typical point differences <0.10 m (∼5% of the 2 m tidal range), and showed consistent spatial gradients in water level from the offshore boundary, through Saldanha Bay, and into the lagoon. At the offshore boundary, TPXO and SWOT sea surface heights agree closely (R2 = 0.86). A ∼26 min phase lag, determined using a lag-correlation analysis, reduces the TPXO–SWOT RMSE from 0.18 m to 0.11 m, indicating that phase differences explain some of the mismatch, with remaining differences likely linked to non-tidal signals. Our results demonstrate that combining passive optical, photon-counting LiDAR, radar interferometry, and global tidal/atmospheric models enables robust, transferrable hydrodynamic modeling in data-scarce coastal systems, offering a cost-effective pathway for monitoring.

title: AVIRIS-NG supervised pan-sharpening of PRISMA imagery in the Cederberg
abstract: The BioSCape campaign run in 2023 within the Greater Cape Floristic Region of South Africa included 5m resolution AVIRIS-NG aerial hyperspectral spectrometry data. 30m resolution PRISMA hyperspectral imagery is available for the same area, and has intermittent revisits, allowing for the detection of changes over time. However, in the highly biodiverse Cape Floristic Region, with single pixels often representing several species or features, PRISMA hyperspectral imagery therefor needs to be sharpened to align to AVIRIS-NG data. Here, a simple ANN pan-sharpening method is implemented to sharpen the PRISMA 30m hyperspectral data using its 5m resolution panchromatic imagery, with AVIRIS 5m imagery as ground truth data.

Ecosystem Resilience to Global Environmental Change in a Biodiversity Hotspot
abstract:
Integrated research across biological scales is vital to understand and anticipate the ecological implications of global environmental change. In particular, the feedbacks between climate, biodiversity, and ecosystem function/services are not well understood. These feedbacks are especially important in fire-prone biomes which cover approximately 40% of Earth’s land surface. There is now a plethora of ecological, natural history, climate, and remotely sensed data available to address this important issue. I explore the potential for climate-biodiversity-ecosystem function feedbacks in the Cape Floristic Region (CFR), a biodiversity hotspot in South Africa. Firstly, I describe an analysis of multi-decadal satellite and field observations. We found that post-fire recovery rate has strong gradients, associated with climate, resulting in faster recovery in regions with higher soil fertility, winter temperature, and summer precipitation. Secondly, we conducted an analysis of the longest-running permanent vegetation plots in the region (44 years) and relate observed changes in diversity and composition to fire history, extreme weather in the first summer after fire, and alien plant species invasion. We found a significant decline in plant diversity over time which was associated with increasingly severe post-fire summer weather events (number of consecutive days with high temperatures and no rain) and alien plant invasion. We also observed a 1◦C increase in maximum temperature tolerance of the species sets unique to each survey, which suggests
there has been selection for species adapted to warmer conditions. Observed differences in the response of major growth forms and fire-response types could drive major shifts in ecosystem structure and function such as altered fire behavior, hydrology, and carbon storage. This is the first example of climate change impacts on biodiversity in this hyperdiverse region and demonstrates an important interaction between extreme weather and disturbance by fire that suggests flammable ecosystems are particularly sensitive to climate change.

abstract:
The Biodiversity Survey of the Cape (BioSCape) is the first US National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) sponsored Biodiversity field campaign which took place in South Africa in late 2023 and incorporated airborne imaging spectroscopy, lidar, and a unique range of field observations and biodiversity measurements across terrestrial and aquatic environments. Airborne data were collected by NASA airborne platforms from four instruments including AVIRIS-NG, PRISM, and HyTES spectrometers and the LVIS laser altimeter. With over 150 Science Team members composed of South African and US-affiliated researchers, data collections will be substantial and heterogeneous especially considering 4 coordinated airborne instruments with flight lines across 45,000km2 of the Greater Cape Floristic Region and supporting field collections. South African partners include the South African Environmental Observation Network (SAEON) and numerous other South African conservation, research, and government institutions.
Here, we describe NASA Earthdata curation and publication of BioSCape airborne derived datasets and field data as well as supportive resources and capacity building. NASA Earthdata is the home for full and open access to NASA's Earth science data collections. As such the full suite of BioSCape airborne datasets and field data collections will be available through NASA’s archive of Earth observations. Much of the airborne and field data will be fully curated and published to NASA Earthdata through the NASA sponsored Oak Ridge National Laboratory Distributed Active Archive Center (ORNL DAAC). However, where BioSCape data are curated through other domain specific NASA DAAC’s or data-appropriate repositories, the NASA DAAC’s will coordinate through controlled Project keywords and NASA’s Common Metadata Repository (CMR) to provide users with a comprehensive listing of BioSCape collections. All datasets published through the ORNL DAAC are provided on the Earthdata Cloud which is NASA’s cloud-based archive of Earth observations and is hosted by Amazon Web Services (AWS). The ORNL DAAC will provide tutorials and training that demonstrate BioSCape airborne and field data access through programmatic discovery and access through application interfaces especially for data on NASA Earthdata Cloud.

abstract:
In Southern Africa, the impacts of anthropogenic activities on biodiversity and ecosystem services are exacerbated by the climate crisis. Rapid land use change and the lack of emphasis on environmentally sustainable agricultural practices has hindered hydrological processes and compromised riverine and aquatic ecosystems biodiversity and long-term ecosystem sustainability. Phytoplankton serve as the foundation of the freshwater food web and include photosynthesizing bacteria (cyanobacteria), plant-like diatoms, dinoflagellates, and green algae. Nutrient run-off from agricultural fertilizers and urban overflows, warm temperatures, abundant light availability and compromised hydrological systems provide an ideal environment for cyanobacteria to flourish. These bloom forming algae can significantly outcompete other phytoplankton classes in warmer and eutrophic waters where they are quick to dominate the freshwater system. Eutrophication and toxic cyanobacteria blooms (cyanoHABs) in the inland waters of the Greater Cape Floristic Region (GCFR) incur significant effects on the biodiversity of the overall phytoplankton assemblage and provide a favorable environment for the overgrowth of floating aquatic vegetation (FAV), which is often invasive and associated with reduced aquatic biodiversity. 
Hyperspectral optical observations are expected to facilitate the improvement of current phytoplankton functional type retrievals significantly, as the sensitivity is sufficient that the distinctive, fine spectral features of different phytoplankton groups can be detected. We will be testing operational and emerging advanced algorithms for use with the BioSCape airborne campaign data. Innovations in optical sensor sensitivity and next generation machine learning capabilities considerably enhance the potential for accurate and rapid detection of phytoplankton, namely the presence, extent, and diversity of cyanobacteria present in cyanoHABs and additionally, invasive FAV. 
The overarching goal of this project is to utilize hyperspectral data, with recently developed and next-generation algorithms, to determine the biodiversity of freshwater systems phytoplankton assemblage with emphasis on genus level distinction, as well as monitor the prevalence and diversity of FAV.

abstract: The Biodiversity Survey of the Cape (BioSCape) aims to understand the structure, function, and composition of terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems in the Greater Cape Floristic Region (GCFR) of South Africa. The research involves the collection and integration of field-based ecological data with data from four airborne instruments, measuring UV/visible to short wavelength infrared (UVSWIR), thermal imaging spectroscopy and laser altimetry LiDAR. Given the GCFR is a complex social-ecological system, there are dynamic non-linear feedbacks between global change, biodiversity change, ecosystem processes and functions, and the resilience and sustainability of nature’s contribution to people.  The BioSCape data set is unique in its size and scope and has potential to provide answers to important ecological and evolutionary questions related to biodiversity, ecosystem services and global change within the GCFR. Given this potential, the BioSCape team seeks to bridge the gap between research and practice by exploring potential applications of the research with end-users and decision-/policy-makers. Here we illustrate the conceptual framing and work to date for the enhancement and documentation of the decision-making relevance of the individual BioSCape research projects with external knowledge holders from South African institutions. By considering the value creation of the data products related to decision-maker needs, our proposed conceptual framing uses the Value Creation Framework and a realist evaluation approach (context, mechanism and outcome) of science applications to address real-world problems. We present progress with a subset of the research teams to date.

abstract: This new BioSCape project based in the Cape Region of South Africa develops a novel, generalizable and species agnostic approach to connect acoustic diversity to animal richness and habitat diversity, as measured by airborne lidar and imaging spectroscopy. In two field campaigns this year, we will deploy a network of independent autonomous recording units (AudioMoths) designed to sample sites across land cover types, fire history and anthropogenic disturbance gradients, along with coincident in situ bird and frog point count measurements conducted by local volunteer ecologists with experience in species identification. With these in situ data and NASA airborne spectral (AVIRIS-NG) and structural (LVIS) measurements collected during the BioSCape multi-team campaign, the project will answer the following questions: 1) What is the relationship among measures of acoustic, spectral and structural diversity and how do those relationships change across spatial scales and vegetation types? and, 2) How do anthropogenic and natural disturbance affect acoustic diversity and habitat quality?

abstract:
BioSCape (www.bioscape.io) is a biodiversity-focussed airborne field campaign taking place in the Greater Cape Floristic Region (GCFR) in the Western Cape of South Africa in October - December 2023. It is an international collaboration between NASA (United States National Aeronautics and Space Administration), SAEON (South African Environmental Observation Network), and SANSA (South African National Space Agency).

The GCFR contains two global biodiversity hotspots? with the richest temperate flora and the third highest marine endemism in the world. The campaign will collect UV/visible to short wavelength infrared (UVSWIR) and thermal imaging spectroscopy and laser altimetry lidar data over terrestrial and aquatic targets using four airborne instruments: AVIRIS-NG, PRISM, LVIS, and HyTES. These airborne data will be accompanied by a range of biodiversity-related field observations on land and in the water. BioSCape’s primary objective is to study the structure, function, and composition of the region’s ecosystems, and to learn about how and why they are changing in time and space. The campaign is organized around three major research themes aimed at understanding: 
1) the distribution and abundance of biodiversity, 
2) the role of biodiversity in ecosystem function, and 
3) the impacts of biodiversity change on ecosystem services. 
Specifically, BioSCape will help us understand where biodiversity is, what it is doing, and why it matters.

In an effort to do equitable and accessible research, all BioSCape data will be open access. We have also made a concerted effort to not perpetuate “parachute science” and have assembled a science team that is half US-based and half SA-based.

title: BioREaCH: Biodiversity-Remote sensing for Estuarine and Coastal Habitat research
abstract: Drivers of estuarine biodiversity and how these will be impacted by climate change vary by region and require precise monitoring. We hypothesize that estuarine essential biodiversity variables vary significantly between climates and hydrogeomorphic settings across the Greater Cape Floristic Region. We endeavor to clarify the relationships between biodiversity, topography, and spectra across the estuaries of the GCFR. This poster details our year-one progress in preparation for field data collection. We have utilized spaceborne sensors, including lidar and optical data, to inform site selection and provide a priori knowledge for understanding the relationships between coastal biodiversity, topography, bathymetry, and spectra. We demonstrate high-resolution satellite-based classifications and preliminary nearshore bathymetry maps for the GCFR. Additionally, we have begun testing some of our hypotheses with spaceborne spectroscopy data to understand likely outcomes for our analysis once aerial data are collected for our study sites. These efforts will lead to our evaluation of how climate change will affect coastal biodiversity in GCFR.

abstract:
This seminar will give an overview of the BioSCape project, including an introduction to its expected datasets. BioSCape is NASA's first biodiversity-focused integrated airborne field campaign. It took place in South Africa in Oct-Nov 2023 and investigates the structure, function, and composition of ecosystems, and how and why they are changing in time and space. BioSCape's airborne dataset is unprecedented in its instrument combination and level of detail, with near complete coverage of the electromagnetic spectrum at high resolution and coincident full-waveform lidar acquisitions. BioSCape's field datasets quantify the diversity of plant communities including alien invasives and kelp, phytoplankton functional types, phylogenetic histories, eDNA in watersheds, bird and frog acoustics, plant functional and spectral traits, blue carbon, and in-water radiometry. BioSCape is committed to facilitating Open Science and all datasets will be delivered to one of NASA's Distributed Archive and Analysis Centers.
South Africa is ideally placed in the crossroads of three ocean basins and three massive and distinct ocean boundary currents. Observations need to be made in such a way that they complement modelling studies and operational activities, such as global weather forecast models, provide insights to unique ocean processes and are able, to some degree, provide the information needed to mitigate against extreme weather and ocean phenomena. 
So where should we deploy ocean observing infrastructure to provide the best bang for our buck? In this presentation we explore the possibilities within the boundary currents around South Africa, look at existing initiatives undertaken by various South African teams, and try to work out where the gaps are.

South Africa Ecological Conservation: Identifying and Mapping Riparian Areas in South Africa with Earth Observations
abstract: Riparian zones are thin strips of wetland that occur along the edges of rivers, lakes, and other water bodies. They provide many ecosystem and societal benefits such as stream bank stabilization, flood control, and habitat stability, making these zones very important areas to preserve and protect. Recognizing the need to accurately map these ecosystems in a cost-effective way, we partnered with the South African National Biodiversity Institute (SANBI) and the Biodiversity Survey of the Cape(BioSCape) to develop a GI methodology using Esri's ArcGIS Pro and data from Landsat 9 Operational Land Imager-2, Sentinel-2 Multispectral Instrument, and the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission to identify potential riparian zones (PRZ) and observed riparian vegetation(ORV) in the Southern Cape and the North West Province of South Africa to estimate the actual riparian vegetation (ARV) within those areas. Potential riparian ecosystems were calculated by utilizing a Topographic Wetness Index (TWI) and a water feature layer, while observed riparian vegetation were calculated by overlaying a Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and TWI. Actual Riparian Vegetation is determined by the overlap of ORV with PRZ and is done with conditional statements; ORV within PRZ is ARV. This method significantly improved a current riparian land cover classification since it combined high resolution optical imagery and topographic data. We anticipate such maps will be used by conservationists and practitioners interested in riparian monitoring and management.

Biodiversity Dynamics and Ecosystem Resilience in Disturbance-Prone Ecosystems: Integrating Field and Remote Sensing Observations
abstract: Ecosystem resilience refers to an ecosystem's ability to withstand environmental disturbances like droughts, storms, wildfires, and other extreme events while maintaining its composition, structure, and function. Improving our understanding of ecological resilience can help with managing and planning for societal resilience. However, a global perspective on how biodiversity and ecosystem functions respond to and recover from environmental perturbations is currently lacking. Since many ecosystems depend on specific disturbance regimes for their persistence (e.g. fire, herbivory, flood), “perturbation” is context-specific, and can be the occurrence or absence of a disturbance event. To systematically map and monitor natural disturbance regimes and compare how different ecosystems respond to stress, integrating field and remote sensing observations is necessary. Remote sensing provides globally and temporally consistent observations to monitor ecosystem dynamics, the occurrence of and responses to events such as wildfire, land-use change, or climate extremes. However, field-based studies are critical to understanding the mechanistic basis of change and how biodiversity can enhance an ecosystem's ability to resist perturbations and recover from them. To produce reliable estimates through time, continuous collection and integration of remote sensing data with field data are necessary. This talk will summarize some challenges of addressing these questions in disturbance-prone ecosystems such as savannas and shrublands, where it is difficult to disentangle natural variability from a state change.  Building mechanistic understanding will enable forecasting and potential management of how ecosystems will respond to future environmental change.

title: Spatial Pattern of Beta Diversity of Plant Species in the Greater Cape Floristic Region of South Africa
abstract: This paper figures out the spatial pattern of biodiversity in the Greater Cape Floristic Region (GCFR) and examines the responses of the plant biodiversity to geodiversity variables, such as temperature, precipitation, seasonality, and elevation. Our study area is the GCFR, well-known for its plant biodiversity – it contains nearly 20% of Africa’s plant species in less than 0.5% of Africa’s total area. In this study we calculate the mean of the local compositional variability by four measures: species richness, beta diversity, nestedness and spatial turnover by using sliding windows, use R to process the species data and Google earth engine to process environmental data by aggregation, standardization and correlation regression. As a result, we got the map of spatial pattern of species richness, mean beta diversity, mean turnover and mean nestedness. In the map of spatial pattern of species richness, more than 2000 species are concentrated in the south-western part of CFR, along the mountain ridges. There are 3 kinds of environmental index which have relatively strong correlation with species richness: annual precipitation (“correlation coefficient (r) = 0.507), annual mean temperature (-0.227), and topography index, such as elevation standard deviation (0.283). And in the map of spatial pattern of mean beta diversity, the higher values (more than 0.25) are concentrated in the south-eastern part of study area. In the map of mean turnover, the location of higher values (more than 0.15) are around the whole south region. The higher values (more than 0.25) of mean nestedness are along the south-north and east-west mountain ridges, with similar location to the magnitude of gradient in the elevation map. Our study suggests that higher geodiversity would contain higher biodiversity, for example, the spatial pattern of most high species richness is distributed in the areas with higher elevation standard deviation. And our finding would contribute to better understanding of deeper mechanism of the interaction between the species and environment, which helps researchers to predict the future distribution of species and design protected area approximately under global climate change.

abstract:
The United States’ National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) is ramping up to its pre-2030 Surface Biology and Geology (SBG) and Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem (PACE) missions, which will see imaging spectroscopy data collected across the world’s land and oceans and distributed openly. This will accompany NASA’s space-borne lidar systems such as the Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation (GEDI) and Ice, Cloud and land Elevation Satellite 2 (ICESat 2), which are both useful for studying vegetation structure. Quantifying the ability of imaging spectroscopy and laser altimeter data to answer questions about the dimensions of biodiversity is therefore an urgent priority, and motivated NASA’s first ever biodiversity-focussed airborne campaign: BioSCape. BioSCape’s airborne sensors collected UVSWIR and TIR imaging spectroscopy and lidar data over terrestrial and aquatic targets in South Africa using four NASA instruments: Airborne Visible Infrared Imaging Spectrometer-Next Generation (AVIRIS-NG), Portable Remote Imaging Spectrometer (PRISM), Hyperspectral Thermal Emission Spectrometer (HyTES), and Land-Vegetation and Ice Sensor (LVIS).
BioSCape, or the Biodiversity Survey of the Cape, took place in the Greater Cape Floristic Region (GCFR) of South Africa in October - November 2023. The GCFR includes the intersections of eight terrestrial and six marine biomes and is known for its extreme topographic and environmental heterogeneity. BioSCape’s primary objective is to understand the structure, function, and composition of the region’s ecosystems, and to learn about how and why they are changing in time and space. The campaign collected remote sensing and field data to study biodiversity to better conserve nature and its contributions to people. BioSCape is organized around three major research themes aimed at understanding:

1. Shifting community composition;
2.Ecosystem disturbance, resilience, and recovery; and
3. Ecosystem function and its contribution to people.

BioSCape is preparing the scientific community for the next generation of earth observation and is pushing the boundaries of what is possible in remote sensing of biodiversity. In this presentation, we will share some of the campaign’s first data products.

title: Trait evolution within the Protea of the Greater Cape Floristic Region of South Africa
abstract: Protea is a diverse genus of woody plants native to Africa, with roughly 112 species, most of which are endemic to the mediterranean shrublands of the Greater Cape Floristic Region (CGFR) of South Africa. Within the region the genus occupies a broad range of environments, ranging from bare rock on mountain tops to sandy flats along the coast. Many of the species also have incredibly narrow ranges and small populations, with some being only a single population. The high diversity and frequent environmental specificity of Protea have resulted in remarkable diversity in form and function, with leaf widths ranging from 1 to 100 millimeters and plant heights ranging from a few centimeters to up to 10 meters. We collected growth characteristics, leaf spectra and spectrally derived functional traits of 67 of the 70 endemic Protea of the GCFR. We combined these traits with a well resolved phylogeny and applied evolutionary models to decipher the mechanisms underpinning the adaptive radiation of the genus across the region. Through this study we seek to better understand long-term evolutionary processes and help monitor the plant diversity in the region.

title: Impacts of Invasive Alien Trees on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Functioning in the Greater Cape Floristic Region
abstract:
Coupled with land use and climate change, biological invasions are a major threat to biodiversity globally. In the Greater Cape Floristic Region (GCFR) of South Africa, a biodiversity hotspot, endemic and rare species are threatened by the proliferation of invasive alien plants, which impact nature’s contributions to people. Specifically, invasive alien trees (IATs) in this region extract more water and increase fuel loads relative to native species, increasing the severity of wildfires and disrupting natural disturbance regimes. More generally, IATs are expected to homogenize landscapes, impacting stability of productivity, among other functions. Monitoring and managing IATs is thus key to ensuring resilient ecosystems. In this work, we combine aerial remote sensing with novel approaches from causal inference, including multiple imputation to account for measurement error, to test ecological theory at scale. First, we combine AVIRIS-NG hyperspectral (380-2510 nm; 5 nm bandwidth; 5 m spatial resolution), LVIS lidar (RH100; 7 m footprint), and field observations to map IATs across a 1000-km2 swath of the GCFR. Second, we investigate the role of biodiversity for a community’s ability to resist invasion and the effects of invasion on biodiversity and ecosystem functioning.
To map the presence of IATs at high resolution, we fuse lidar and hyperspectral products to separate invaded vs. native vegetation via machine learning classification, achieving high-accuracy (>80% accuracy for 800 points) due to differences in NIR reflectance (~800 nm), SWIR reflectance (~1600 nm) and canopy height between IATs and native species. Among IATs, classification accuracy varies significantly, with only moderate separability among gum and wattle. Nonetheless, with high accuracy in distinguishing IATs from native stands, we address three hypotheses relating to invasion status across the landscape: 1) Diversity decreases invasibility, 2) IATs increase alpha-diversity, but decrease beta-diversity, and 3) IATs negatively impact ecosystem functioning, including productivity and its stability, both directly and indirectly via impacts to diversity. Overall, our inferences confirm ecological theory, indicating both the utility of remote sensing for monitoring IATs and the need for management that addresses IAT impacts.

title: Enhancing Mediterranean Biodiversity Monitoring in South Africa via Machine Learning and Cost-Effective UAS Imagery
abstract: The Greater Cape Floristic Region (GCFR) of South Africa is renowned for its extraordinary plant diversity and high rates of endemism. This hyperdiverse ecosystem, however, is under threat from habitat loss, altered fire regimes, and invasive species. Consequently, developing effective monitoring and management strategies are crucial for its conservation. While satellite remote sensing offers a promising avenue for biodiversity monitoring, its utility is often limited by the spatial resolution of available imagery. The GCFR's open shrublands cause soils, stems, and other surfaces to significantly influence the observed reflectance. Vegetation conditions vary widely due to seasonal changes, natural disturbances like fire or drought, and long-term post-disturbance recovery. These dynamics are further complicated by the region's inherent species diversity. In the past decade, researchers have increasingly utilized unmanned aerial systems (UAS), or drones, which provide high spatial resolution imagery, capable of capturing fine-scale vegetation dynamics. Here we aim to demonstrate the efficacy of high-resolution UAS multispectral imagery in classifying post-fire areas and mapping diversity within the shrubland fynbos biome of the GCFR. Evaluating this fire-prone system as a function of the time since the last fire is essential for understanding its ecological dynamics and resilience. Our methodology is grounded in the spectral variation hypothesis (SVH) and leverages optimal spectral and textural features derived from UAS imagery to distinguish between different burned areas, followed by an estimation of alpha diversity at fine scales. We employed machine learning techniques and the sequential feature selection (SFS) method to identify optimal spectral and textural features to classify different burned areas within the imagery. A support vector machine (SVM) classifier achieved promising classification results, with an overall accuracy of 96%, and a precision, recall, and F1 score of 97.47%. Utilizing these optimal features and the Shannon diversity index (H) from ground truth samples, we applied a similarity metric, namely the Euclidean distance, to map alpha diversity across varied burned areas within the fynbos biome. This study highlights the value of using cost-effective remote sensing technologies, like UAS, in ecological research to classify post-fire burned areas through spectral dynamics and assess biodiversity status, providing insights into post-disturbance recovery.

title: Mapping Soil Salinity across Coastal Wetlands with Airborne Imaging Spectroscopy
abstract: Soil salinity is a key environmental control on vegetation community composition and plant stress. In the context of global change, coastal wetland environments are experiencing salinity changes induced by relative sea level rise as well as altered storm patterns. These shifts in salinity regimes can diminish plant productivity and carbon storage capabilities in wetlands, and even cause plant dieback, exacerbating wetland loss. To quantify wetland processes in the global carbon cycle, it is essential to develop a framework linking salinity changes to plant stress, community composition changes, and wetland carbon fluxes. Targeted high-resolution observations with airborne imaging spectrometers in concert with in-situ soil sampling and spectroscopic measurements provide the best opportunity to develop these analytical tools. We collected data in 2023 as part of NASA’s BioSCape campaign in South Africa’s estuaries, including field data quantifying wetland vegetation composition and local salinity measurements in coordination with overflights by the Airborne Visible/Infrared Imaging Spectrometer—Next Generation (AVIRIS-NG). Additional data was collected in Carpinteria, California, in April 2024 by AVIRIS-3, with coincident in situ soil samples—processed in a lab setting to measure salt content—and visible-shortwave infrared (VSWIR) reflectance measurements. A model to estimate soil salinity based on reflectance was developed from these data (n=32, R2=0.898, mean absolute error = 0.005 g salt per g dry soil). We then used multiple endmember spectral mixture analysis (MESMA) to estimate soil percent cover per pixel and applied our model to both sites in the applicable pixels. In doing so, we produced accurate maps of wetland soil salinity and investigated community composition as a function of salinity, while also assessing the potential for a generalizable salinity algorithm.

title: Optical variability of dissolved organic material within coastal and inland water bodies around the Greater Cape Floristic Region, South Africa
abstract: The Greater Cape Floristic Region of southern Africa is outlined by coastal bays that receive terrigenous dissolved organic matter (DOM) from rivers draining dammed reservoirs. Optical properties of these coastal waters can provide insight into DOM concentration and quality, and enable monitoring of DOM dynamics from remote sensing platforms. As part of NASA's BioSCape field campaign (October-November 2023), we examined optical properties of three coastal bays: St. Helena Bay, Walker Bay, and Algoa Bay, and four inland water bodies, in relation to DOM biogeochemistry and carbon cycling. We measured the absorption properties of colored dissolved organic matter (CDOM), including the absorption coefficient at 300 nm (ag,300) and the spectral slope from 275-295 nm (S275-295), as well as fluorescence excitation-emission matrices (EEMs) to better characterize the optical complexity associated with terrestrial influences on these coastal margins. We found generally low ag,300 values (0.5 – 2.8 m-1) in the bays, and much higher values (25 – 71 m-1) in the inland water bodies and, conversely, higher S275-295 values in the bays (0.020 – 0.031 nm-1) than in the inland waters (0.012 – 0.019 nm-1). Additionally, we fit a four component Parallel Factor Analysis (PARAFAC) model which captured 96% of fluorescence variability within the dataset. Two components were associated with terrestrially derived humic material, and two resembled protein-like degradation products indicative of bacterial utilization. Coastal samples were mostly composed (> 75%) of protein-like products, while inland water samples were mostly composed (> 77%) of terrigenous humic materials. For all components, fluorescence intensities were significantly higher (t-test, p < 0.005) in the inland waters than in the coastal waters. Finally, we used coincident in situ remote sensing reflectance and ag,300 measurements to optimize a multilinear regression algorithm designed for monitoring ag,300 using Sentinel-3 OLCI. Timeseries analysis in each of the three bays revealed extended periods of drought punctuated by heavy bouts of precipitation over each rivers’ watersheds, which had a significant impact on CDOM distribution across the land-water continuum.

title: Enabling Coastal wetland monitoring across scales with lidar, imaging spectroscopy, and very high-resolution satellite imagery.
abstract: Coastal wetlands provide critical ecosystem services, including biodiversity, carbon sequestration, and flood protection. Species and community-level mapping efforts have been limited in scope. As part of the BioSCape science team, we collected field data that overlapped temporally and spatially with the airborne data collection. We used these data and satellite imagery to map coastal wetlands and the impact of tidal range and relative sea level rise on community distribution. Across the 83 estuaries mapped, We mapped a total of 9130.311±1596.69 ha of salt marsh & reed beds and 1718.6 ± 234.25 ha of Submerged Aquatic Vegetation (SAV). These classes were mapped with an overall accuracy of 90.8%. We also spatially predicted species diversity for all estuaries, finding that 68.7 percent had some extent of high coastal wetland species richness (>5 coastal wetland species). In total, we mapped 1464.5 ha of high coastal wetland species richness. In addition to our earth observation analysis, we calculated relative sea level rise trends and tidal amplitude for twenty tidal gauges across the region. We found tidal amplitude to be a significant driver of salt marsh extent, explaining 33.6% of the variation in salt marsh extent (F (1,19) = 9.62, p = .005). We highlight the novel utilization of the BioSCape airborne data for understanding coastal wetlands. 1) We analyzed coastal wetland vegetation by comparing the structural characteristics of Swartvlei and Langebaan with Land, Vegetation, and Ice Sensor (LVIS), field data, and a coastal DTM. We found significant structural differences between estuaries and vegetation types. 2) We map species distributions across the coastal wetland extent of Langebaan Lagoon with in situ spectral signatures and Multiple Endmember Spectral Mixture Analysis (MESMA). Our study demonstrates the utilization of cutting-edge airborne datasets with satellite remote sensing to improve our understanding of coastal wetland biodiversity and develop critical baselines for future long-term monitoring in support of the Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) and Sustainable Development Goals (SDG).

title: Hyperspectral optical signatures of canopy-forming macroalgae in the Western Cape province of South Africa
abstract: Kelp forests support the biodiversity and high rates of production found in the subtidal coastal habitats of the Western Cape province of South Africa, in part, by providing three-dimensional structure and food to many organisms. Kelp forest habitats also confer social and economic services to human populations. Temporal variability in the regional distributions, abundance, and physiological state of the region’s canopy-forming (both floating and submerged) kelp taxa—namely Ecklonia, Macrocystis, and Laminaria—modify the ecosystem services provided by kelp forests to the region, but gaps remain in the coverage of kelp forest monitoring programs. Recent remote sensing advances support new opportunities to improve the monitoring and study of the region’s kelp forests using airborne and satellite observations, but require field activities to validate remote sensing products. A hyperspectral optical field survey of canopy-forming kelps was conducted during November 2023 as part of the NASA Biodiversity Survey of the Cape (BioSCape) campaign, with the objective of characterizing spectral signatures of Western Cape kelp forests and quantifying spectral variability related to taxonomy and physiological condition. Kelp forests were sampled at 15 coastal sites between St. Helena Bay and Cape Agulhas in coordination with contemporaneous airborne and satellite observations. The remote sensing observations include hyperspectral maps obtained from airborne surveys using the NASA next-generation Airborne Visible/Infrared Imaging Spectrometer (AVIRIS-NG) system and multispectral maps obtained from very-high resolution Planet SkySat satellite imagery. Ground samples were assessed using field spectroscopy combined with laboratory elemental analysis to relate spectral characteristics across sites with taxonomic and physiological differences. Preliminary findings of the NASA BioSCape field and remote sensing kelp forest surveys are presented, and upcoming plans for follow-on collaborative research activities are described.

title: Optimizing Bio-Optical Field Data Collections for Airborne Campaigns: Insights from NASA's BioSCape program in South Africa
abstract: BioSCape is an integrated field and airborne campaign that used airborne hyperspectral data from AVIRIS-NG and PRISM aimed at mapping the biodiversity of the Cape Floristic Region of South Africa, one of the world's 36 biodiversity hotspots. It was conducted in the Fall of 2023, only a few months before the launch of NASA’s Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem (PACE), a mission equipped with an advanced suite of hyperspectral radiometric and polarimetric instruments, aimed at revolutionizing biodiversity mapping and ecosystem change analysis. The success of PACE for developing products for mapping aquatic biodiversity and evaluating ecosystem change studies, will depend on well-designed field campaigns that maximize bio-optical data collections, essential for validating remote measurements of water-leaving radiances. Data collected during our BioSCape survey, and the lessons learned in designing and coordinating field and airborne campaigns in transitional coastal waters are of relevance to PACE and its hyperspectral capabilities especially in coastal waters. This presentation will discuss field sampling strategies employed by us to overcome the challenges of sampling in ecologically distinct bays along South Africa’s long coastline. Measurements were undertaken on two coastal survey vessels, one that allowed us to make optical and biogeochemical measurements continuously and at discrete stations along a single flight line, and the other perpendicular to the flight path, that permitted optical measurements across several flight lines. This sampling strategy planned in close coordination with the aircraft team helped maximize our bio-optical and biogeochemical data collections across diverse bio-optical water types which were vital to the campaign's success.

title: Toward Validating Virtual Models of Complex Shrubland Ecosystems for Next-Generation Airborne LiDAR Studies
abstract: The application of airborne and spaceborne light detection and ranging (LiDAR) for characterizing and monitoring low‑stature ecosystems, such as- rangelands, wetlands (bogs, fens, swamps, marshes), and polar ecosystems (tundra, taiga), presents unique challenges compared to its established use in forested environments. These challenges stem primarily from the short, dense nature of vegetation and the limited ability of LiDAR to discriminate between ground and vegetation returns in low-stature environments. Real world assessment of these limitations is difficult due to the scarcity of repeat surveys with multiple sensor configurations in such ecosystems. Physics-based simulation tools, like Digital Imaging and Remote Sensing Image Generation (DIRSIG), offer a way to overcome such limitations by generating realistic multimodal LiDAR datasets and exploring system performance boundaries. In this study, we developed multiple post-fire virtual scenes representing different levels of maturity, for the highly diverse fynbos shrubland biome present in South Africa’s Cape Floristic Region (CFR). These scenes were constructed using realistic 3D models of individual species, derived from field surveys, that combined spectral and structural measurements. We focus on the structural validation of these virtual scenes by comparing structural traits derived from high-density simulated LiDAR data with corresponding traits measured from field-based structure‑from‑motion (SfM) surveys. This validation establishes the reliability of the virtual scenes and lays the groundwork for their use in future studies aimed at informing next-generation LiDAR system specifications for complex low-stature ecosystems.

title: BIOSCape - Mapping of phytoplankton functional types from space in support of coastal resource management and decision support activities
abstract: Sheltered bays along South Africa's coastline are highly productive and its phytoplankton communities extraordinarily biodiverse. This biodiversity of organisms at the bottom of the food chain, vital for fisheries, tourism, and biodiversity, is facing increasing threats from climate change, especially extreme temperatures, hypoxia etc that are favoring outbreaks of Harmful Algal Blooms (HABs). Monitoring these detrimental changes, critical for stakeholders, remains challenging due to the ecological complexity and varying environmental conditions. As part of our BioSCAPE study, we developed a hyperspectral radiometric method that is based on the Multi-pigment inversion model (MuPI), to map the spatial distribution of phytoplankton functional types (PFTs) across environmental gradients within three ecologically distinct and socio-economically vital bays, i.e. St. Helena, Walker and Algoa. MuPI takes advantage of the unique hyperspectral remote sensing reflectance (Rrs) signals arising from phytoplankton pigment variability to detect specific PFTs. Field data, that includes optical, microscopic, phytoplankton pigment, and e-DNA data collected during the BioSCape campaign (Oct.-Nov. 2023), were used disentangle phytoplankton Rrs signatures from other seawater components like minerals and organic matter. The residual Rrs signals were then analyzed to detect different pigments, allowing discrimination of specific PFTs. MuPI was then applied to hyperspectral AVIRIS-NG and PRISM sesnors that were flown during the BIOSCape field campaign. Initial results show diatom dominance in Algoa Bay and a higher prominence of dinoflagellates in St. Helena Bay, which is consistent with the in-situ observations. Additionally, blooms of Mesodinium sp. in St. Helena Bay and Red Noctiluca scintillans in Walker Bay were captured and modeled. The model was also extended to other satellite data (Landsat OLI, Sentinel-3 OLCI, and PACE) to generate satellite maps of PFTs with associated uncertainties. These satellite maps will enhance understanding of biodiversity distribution and abundance along South Africa's coast, shedding light on the feedbacks between global change, biodiversity shifts, and ecosystem services.

Monitoring Dimensions of Biodiversity in a Mega-Diverse Region of Southern Africa: from Traits to Communities to Ecosystems
abstract: The Greater Cape Floristic Region (GCFR) of South Africa includes marine and terrestrial biomes with species diversity rivaling mega-diverse tropical rainforests in a compact area (300x700km). Extinction risk studies suggest that GCFR species are among the most vulnerable to climate change over the next 50 years. I present a scoping proposal commissioned by NASA to develop a field campaign to measure and monitor the distribution and abundance of biodiversity with new remotely-sensed data and the rich historical data in this region. I will summarize the central questions to be addressed by this field campaign and lay out the proposed study design to integrate satellite, airborne, and in situ data collection. Our plan centers around the collection of new hyperspectral imagery from AVIRIS-NG, PRISM, and HyTES spectrometers combined with the LVIS laser altimeter. These data will be collected at approximately 20 m spatial resolution across much of the GCFR and nearby aquatic and marine ecosystems. These data will then be combined with existing and new observations of the spatial distribution of community composition and functional traits to enable high resolution mapping and modeling of several essential biodiversity variables (EBVs) including species distributions, functional traits (including leaf properties), and three-dimensional canopy structure. Given the wealth of available independent in situ data available that can be brought to bear, the GCFR is an ideal system to fully evaluate the capabilities of remote-sensing technology to characterize biodiversity patterns across diverse landscapes in a relatively compact geographic area. In combination with the rich historical data and well-developed ecological understanding in this region, these new observations will enable detailed exploration into the drivers and mechanisms of change including the feedbacks from changing biodiversity to regional climate, disturbance, post-fire recovery, freshwater provisioning, and other ecosystem services.

title: Remote Sensing for Biodiversity: Insights from the BioSCape Campaign
abstract: BioSCape (Biodiversity Survey of the Cape) is NASA’s first biodiversity-focused airborne and field campaign, designed to advance understanding of ecosystem structure, function, and composition, and how these are changing over time and space in South Africa’s Greater Cape Floristic Region. This international collaboration involving ~160 US and South African scientists across 19 sub-projects produced an unprecedented, open-access dataset spanning 45,000 km², integrating imaging spectroscopy (AVIRIS-NG, PRISM, HyTES), LiDAR (LVIS, ELMAP-V), and extensive ground data from ~2,600 plots. Data are publicly archived at ORNL DAAC and accessible via a cloud computing environment, fostering open science and reproducibility. In this presentation, we will summarize the results to date across the BioSCape project, highlighting key scientific outcomes from both terrestrial and aquatic landscapes. We will also discuss some of the broader implications of the project, including laying the groundwork for achieving ethical and equitable benefit-sharing via compliance with the Nagoya Protocol. A core principle of BioSCape is "use-inspired science," which involves co-developing research questions with local partners to directly address pressing conservation and resource management challenges. This ensures that our scientific findings translate into actionable data products for decision-makers in South Africa and globally. For example, BioSCape's data and products are already informing conservation and resource management efforts, including kelp range maps for ecosystem classification and woody invasive alien plant maps that feed into national ecosystem condition assessments. The project's contributions have already been recognized in the 2024 State of Environment Outlook Report for the Western Cape Province.

title: The Spectrum of Life: A short film about the Biodiversity Survey of the Cape
abstract:
All organisms have a unique fingerprint, with diverse communities on land and in water reflecting sunlight in distinctive ways. These fingerprints can provide clues about an ecosystem’s characteristics, such as how biodiverse it is, how it functions, which communities thrive in particular environments, how much chlorophyll and other pigments are present in a lake and how much water is held in a forest canopy. The link between spectral fingerprints and ecosystem characteristics unlocks the potential to measure biodiversity using NASA’s next-generation of remote sensing technology, including imaging spectroscopy.
The Spectrum of Life is a short documentary about how the BioSCape project is exploring the use of imaging spectroscopy and other tools to measure biodiversity in one of the most biodiverse regions on the planet - South Africa’s Greater Cape Floristic Region. The film features insights from and experiences with local and international researchers collaborating to push the boundaries of global biodiversity science - all weaved together with an audiovisual celebration of the region’s exceptional diversity.

Biodiversity Dynamics and Ecosystem Resilience in Disturbance-Prone Ecosystems: Integrating Field and Remote Sensing Observations
abstract: Ecosystem resilience refers to an ecosystem's ability to withstand environmental disturbances like droughts, storms, wildfires, and other extreme events while maintaining its composition, structure, and function. Improving our understanding of ecological resilience can help with managing and planning for societal resilience. However, a global perspective on how biodiversity and ecosystem functions respond to and recover from environmental perturbations is currently lacking. Since many ecosystems depend on specific disturbance regimes for their persistence (e.g. fire, herbivory, flood), “perturbation” is context-specific, and can be the occurrence or absence of a disturbance event. To systematically map and monitor natural disturbance regimes and compare how different ecosystems respond to stress, integrating field and remote sensing observations is necessary. Remote sensing provides globally and temporally consistent observations to monitor ecosystem dynamics, the occurrence of and responses to events such as wildfire, land-use change, or climate extremes. However, field-based studies are critical to understanding the mechanistic basis of change and how biodiversity can enhance an ecosystem's ability to resist perturbations and recover from them. To produce reliable estimates through time, continuous collection and integration of remote sensing data with field data are necessary. This talk will summarize some challenges of addressing these questions in disturbance-prone ecosystems such as savannas and shrublands, where it is difficult to disentangle natural variability from a state change.  Building mechanistic understanding will enable forecasting and potential management of how ecosystems will respond to future environmental change.

title: Biodiversity Survey of the Cape ( BioSCape )
abstract: We provide an overview of the first ever NASA Biodiversity campaign, to be flown in 2023. Incorporating airborne imaging spectroscopy, lidar, and field observations, the campaign will explore the structure, composition, function and threats to biodiversity across South Africa’s Greater Cape Floristic Region (GCFR), including freshwater, coastal and marine environments. The GCFR contains two Global Biodiversity Hotspots with the richest temperate flora and the third highest marine endemism in the world. The field campaign includes collection of new hyperspectral data ranging from UV to thermal wavelengths acquired by PRISM, AVIRIS-NG, and HyTES spectrometers combined with the LVIS laser altimeter (LiDAR) aboard the NASA GIII and GV aircraft. These remotely sensed data will be combined with existing and new field observations of the spatial distribution of species, ecosystems, and their traits, processes (e.g. fire) and threats (e.g. invasive alien species) to enable high resolution mapping of biodiversity, functional traits, and three-dimensional structure across environmental gradients and times-since-disturbance. The campaign is working with local research and conservation stakeholders to address locally and globally relevant questions organized around three major themes: 1) the distribution and abundance of biodiversity, 2) the role of biodiversity in ecosystem function, and 3) the impacts of biodiversity change on ecosystem services. This focus represents an important paradigm shift from previous NASA field campaigns, which were primarily biogeochemical, toward an approach for measuring and understanding functional, phylogenetic, and taxonomic biological diversity as key components of ecosystem function.

title: Bringing ‘parachute science’ back to Earth to improve remote sensing of biodiversity for all
abstract:
The most important scientific challenges facing us today are global in scope and interdisciplinary in nature.   Understanding and addressing environmental problems such as global climate change and biodiversity loss will require collaboration and trust within and across the international research community.   International research endeavours have the potential to engage scientists from around the world to address these questions and develop innovative solutions.  But, they also have the potential to alienate, discourage, and hinder progress through ‘parachute science’ in which scientists, often from wealthier nations, visit a location, collect data, and publish results with minimal engagement with the local scientists and/or decision-makers.  The growing use of remote sensing has the potential to exacerbate these issues through remote data collection, interpretation, and analysis.  This practice ignores local traditional knowledge and scientific expertise, reinforces existing global inequities, and reduces uptake. By ignoring critical local context and expertise, the ultimate consequences may be reduced impact of science in the local country, and lower quality science.  
Avoiding parachute science has implications not only for international science and collaborations, but also for issues of justice, equity, diversity, and inclusion (JEDI) in the US and more broadly.  Representation of racial and ethnic minorities in the geosciences remains abysmally low. Integrating local and traditional voices and perspectives through collaborative research is one way to challenge global inequities and increase diversity that can be mirrored in our student populations and future workforce. It is important to have these conversations now, as the rate of international research is increasing, particularly within the biodiversity community. A set of best practices is needed to structure projects to maximize meaningful engagement and collaboration (including opportunities for data sharing, co-authorship, reciprocal visits and training). The question is, how do we do this well?
In this workshop, we will discuss the challenges of developing bi- and multilateral international research projects, with a specific focus on avoiding ‘parachute science’ in projects related to remote sensing of the environment and biodiversity. The workshop will kick off with a panel discussion involving individuals that have had experiences with international research projects in the past. Then, using the recently funded NASA BioSCape program (bioscape.io) as an example, we will encourage participants to brainstorm and co-design strategies to enhance scientific engagement. Lastly, we will also discuss potential indicators that assess the integrity of international research projects that participants can use in their own collaborations.
